ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: The pedigree chart of a family with two single-gene genetic diseases, A and B, is shown in the figure. Disease A is a certain familial hereditary tumor, controlled by alleles A/a; disease B is phenylketonuria, caused by a lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase, controlled by alleles B/b, and the two pairs of genes are inherited independently. Researchers performed PCR amplification on the two genes of members of this family, and the gel electrophoresis chart of amplification products of some members is shown in the figure. Analyze according to the figure, assuming that the probability of being a carrier of disease B in the normal population is 1/75, if Ⅲ-5 marries an unrelated normal man, what is the probability of giving birth to an affected child?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: The pedigree chart of a family with two single-gene genetic diseases, A and B, is shown in the figure. Disease A is a certain familial hereditary tumor, controlled by alleles A/a; disease B is phenylketonuria, caused by a lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase, controlled by alleles B/b, and the two pairs of genes are inherited independently. Researchers performed PCR amplification on the two genes of members of this family, and the gel electrophoresis chart of amplification products of some members is shown in the figure. Analyze according to the figure, assuming that the probability of being a carrier of disease B in the normal population is 1/75, if Ⅲ-5 marries an unrelated normal man, what is the probability of giving birth to an affected child?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the pedigree chart, female I-1 and male I-2 are both marked with diagonal lines, indicating that they have disease A; among their children, II-3 and II-5 are normal individuals. II-5 marries normal female II-6 and has two normal females, III-4 and III-5. In the pedigree, III-2 is marked with horizontal lines, indicating that she has only disease B. The gel electrophoresis chart shows the amplification bands of the A/a gene and B/b gene of some members; among the amplification bands of the B/b gene, disease B patient III-2 has only the pathogenic b band, according to which the position of the b band can be determined; I-1 and I-2 both have two bands, B and b, at the B/b locus, and are Bb; II-6 has only the normal B band at the B/b locus, and is BB. Then reason: I-1 and I-2 both have disease A but have normal children II-3 and II-5, indicating that disease A is treated as autosomal dominant inheritance. III-5 and her parents II-5 and II-6 do not have disease A in the pedigree, and she marries a normal man, so the probability that her children have disease A is 0. Disease B is phenylketonuria, analyzed as autosomal recessive inheritance. From electrophoresis it can be known that I-1 and I-2 are Bb×Bb, and II-5 does not show disease B, therefore the conditional probability that II-5 is carrier Bb is 2/3. II-6 is BB, so the probability that III-5 obtains the b allele from II-5 is (2/3)×(1/2)=1/3, that is, the probability that III-5 is a carrier of disease B is 1/3. The question stem gives that the probability that the unrelated normal man is a carrier of disease B is 1/75. If both parties are Bb, the probability of giving birth to a bb child with disease B is 1/4. Therefore, the total probability of giving birth to an affected child is 0 + (1/3)×(1/75)×(1/4)=1/900.
